---
title: "Question 3: Would Its Headline Finding Survive a Push?"
---

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/common.R")
fr <- readRDS("data/fragility.rds")
cal <- readRDS("data/calibration.rds")
fc <- readRDS("data/forecast.rds")
cv <- fr$curve
b <- fr$base
ps <- fr$plus_size
sd_or <- fr$seed_or
fal <- fr$falsifyr
iso <- cal$metrics[cal$metrics$method == "Isotonic-calibrated", ]
raw <- cal$metrics[cal$metrics$method == "Raw VendorScore", ]
full <- fc$results[1, ]
n_inc <- sum(readRDS("data/models.rds")$bank_data$incident)
```

## The question

NorthPoint built its own logistic regression, the bank's incident-association model, from
its panel. Its headline: vendors without a current SOC 2 Type II report have about twice
the odds of an incident. That finding now supports a contract policy. How small a change
makes it disappear?

## Method in brief

**Pre-registered definition of a "kill":** the smallest perturbation under which the
no-SOC-2 coefficient loses statistical significance at the 5% level, using standard errors
clustered by vendor (each vendor appears 48 times, so ordinary standard errors overstate
precision).

We apply it two ways. A *specification curve* re-estimates the odds ratio across 32
reasonable model choices. A *smallest-kill search* looks for the least damaging change,
including greedily deleting the vendor-months that most prop up the estimate.

The `falsifyr` package runs its within-model attacks on the same model.^[`falsifyr` does
not use vendor-clustered standard errors and cannot add an omitted variable, so the
pre-registered kill is a hand-built loop. `falsifyr` supplies the within-model attacks.]
Alternatives, such as E-values, ask about unmeasured confounding without naming it.

## Findings

```{r}
#| label: fig-speccurve
#| fig-cap: "No-SOC-2 odds ratio across 32 model choices, ordered by size, with 95% vendor-clustered intervals. Dashed line: the true value, 1.25."
#| fig-alt: "Dot-and-interval plot of 32 odds ratios in two clusters: about 1.3 with vendor size included, about 2.0 to 2.4 without it, with a horizontal line at 1.25."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.4
cv$label <- ifelse(cv$vendor_size, "Vendor size included", "Vendor size omitted")
ggplot(cv, aes(rank, or, colour = label)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = fr$true_or, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), size = 0.35) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(okabe_ito[c("blue", "vermillion")])) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.8, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 3), labels = c("0.8", "1", "1.25", "1.5", "2", "3")) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "Specification (ordered by odds ratio)",
       y = "Odds ratio for no SOC 2 (log scale)", colour = NULL)
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the plot.** Each dot is the answer from one reasonable way of building the
model. Height is the estimated increase in the odds of an incident for vendors without SOC 2.
A value of 1 means no effect. The vertical line through each dot shows the plausible range.
The dashed line is the true effect, which we know because the data are simulated.

**What the plot tells you.** The dots form two separate groups. Every model that leaves
out vendor size gives an estimate near 2 to 2.4; every model that includes it gives
about 1.3, close to the truth. Other choices (the type of model, trimming outliers,
dropping controls) matter far less. One decision drives the result. Larger vendors are both more
likely to hold SOC 2 and safer, and leaving size out credits SOC 2 with that safety.
:::

All `r sum(!cv$vendor_size & cv$significant)` specifications without vendor size are significant
(odds ratios `r num(min(cv$or[!cv$vendor_size]))` to `r num(max(cv$or[!cv$vendor_size]))`). None of the `r sum(cv$vendor_size)` that include it is
(`r num(min(cv$or[cv$vendor_size]))` to `r num(max(cv$or[cv$vendor_size]))`).

```{r}
#| label: fig-kill
#| fig-cap: "Smallest kill: clustered p-value as incident vendor-months are deleted. Adding vendor size alone (diamond) crosses the 5% line with nothing deleted."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of p-value rising as rows are deleted, crossing 0.05 at the point marked, and a diamond above 0.05 at zero deletions for the model with vendor size."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
dp <- fr$deletion_path
ggplot(dp, aes(removed, p)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_line(colour = okabe_ito[["blue"]], linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(colour = okabe_ito[["blue"]], size = 1.6) +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(removed = 0, p = ps$p), shape = 18, size = 5,
             colour = okabe_ito[["vermillion"]]) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_number(drop0trailing = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = "Incident vendor-months deleted (greedy search)",
       y = "Clustered p-value (log scale)")
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the plot.** The blue line removes, one at a time, the incidents at vendors
without SOC 2 that most support the finding, and tracks how convincing the result remains.
Higher means weaker evidence. Above the dashed line the result is no longer
statistically significant. The diamond shows the result when we simply add vendor size.

**What the plot tells you.** Throwing away real incidents erodes the finding slowly: it takes
`r fr$kill_rows` deletions, about `r pct(fr$kill_rows / n_inc, 0)` of all `r n_inc` incidents, before it fails. A single better
model choice does the same job with nothing deleted. The finding is sturdy against data
noise but not against a flawed model.
:::

The deletion count is an upper bound on the true smallest data kill, since the search is
greedy. `falsifyr` found no kill at all (verdict: `r tolower(fal$verdict)`), but cannot test the
better model that matters here. A tool that only perturbs a model never reveals that the
model itself was missing something.

**Seed sensitivity.** We re-ran the simulation under seeds 1 to 40 with the final
parameters. The naive odds ratio ranged from `r num(min(sd_or$naive_or))` to `r num(max(sd_or$naive_or))` (median `r num(median(sd_or$naive_or))`), and was
significant in `r sum(sd_or$naive_p < 0.05)` of 40. With vendor size included, it ranged from
`r num(min(sd_or$adj_or))` to `r num(max(sd_or$adj_or))` (median `r num(median(sd_or$adj_or))`) and was significant in only `r sum(sd_or$adj_p < 0.05)`. With about 200 incidents, a
single sample can move the answer a lot, so the exact "2×" is itself fragile, even though the upward bias from omitting size is systematic.

## So what

The "2× odds" headline reflects confounding, not a robust effect of SOC 2: in this
sample the size-adjusted estimate is `r num(ps$or)` (interval `r num(ps$low)` to `r num(ps$high)`), not distinguishable from no effect at 5%.
The model was built to describe incident associations, then reused to justify a contract
policy. The guidance flags use beyond a model's intended purpose (§IV, Model Use) and
calls for effective challenge and alternative assumptions (§III, §V). The challenge here
was a single added variable.

This too is partial validation: a robust association would still be an association, not a
cause, and the page cannot say whether SOC 2 reduces risk.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scorecard
#| tbl-cap: "Series scorecard: NorthPoint's measured results and the responses suggested by the guidance's vocabulary."
score <- data.frame(
  Test = c("Calibration", "Forecast dominance", "Fragility"),
  Question = c("Honest probabilities?", "Beats a simple model?", "Robust headline?"),
  Result = c(
    sprintf("Top-scored group predicted %s vs observed %s; recalibration gains are small and unclear (Brier %s to %s), and undercount incidents.",
            pct(cal$reliability$predicted[cal$reliability$score == "Raw VendorScore" & cal$reliability$bin == 10]),
            pct(cal$reliability$observed[cal$reliability$score == "Raw VendorScore" & cal$reliability$bin == 10]),
            num(raw$brier, 4), num(iso$brier, 4)),
    sprintf("MSE %s lower than the 12-month average, not significant (p = %s).",
            pct(1 - full$mse_vs / full$mse_naive, 0), pval(full$dm_p)),
    sprintf("Odds ratio %s falls to %s (p = %s) once vendor size is added.",
            num(b$or), num(ps$or), num(ps$p))),
  Response = c("Overlay: recalibrate output; set thresholds, refresh regularly",
               "Closer monitoring; raise with vendor; ask for development evidence; keep contingency plan",
               "Limit use: not a basis for contract policy; document the exception"))
knitr::kable(score)
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the table.** One row per question. The "Result" column is what we measured
at NorthPoint. The "Response" column is the action that sound practice suggests, in the
guidance's own vocabulary: an overlay adjusts a model's output without changing the
model, and limits on use restrict what a result may be used for.

**What the table tells you.** None of the three tests found the vendor model or the bank's
own finding to be clean. These results do not, on their own, argue for scrapping VendorScore. Each calls for a
proportionate response: adjust, watch, or limit. The weakest item is the bank's own
finding, not the vendor's model.
:::

## Committee action

Sound practice suggests documenting the SOC 2 finding as an exception to its intended
purpose: not a basis for contract policy until a size-adjusted analysis supports it. The April 2026 interagency *Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management* does not prescribe this; it is a judgement for the committee.
